reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Cranes, Dedicated and Universal Rigs, Leads, Templates, Helmets, Hammer Cushions, and Pile Cushions
sections.summary: Crane, leads, hammer and helmet are the primary driving system parts. Crawler cranes are most common; truck and rough terrain cranes have restricted side lifting. Swinging leads are the most widely used configuration and the historical penalty on them is not justified. Templates go within 5 ft of cutoff or water elevation. Helmets about 0.1 to 0.2 in. larger than the pile. Proprietary hammer cushions last up to 200 hours; wood pile cushions at least 4 in., new and dry for each pile.
sections.body: Chapter introduction (p. 333): the driving system is also a measuring instrument for nominal resistance. 15.1 (pp. 333-336): crawler cranes have good mobility, wide-base stability and a 360 degree hoisting radius, can carry the power pack or compressor as counterweight, are trucked in pieces and need firm ground or crane mats. Truck (mobile) cranes travel under their own power but cannot walk with heavy loads, use outriggers, cannot carry the power source and have restricted side lifting. Rough terrain cranes set up fast and are more mobile in difficult terrain but have very restricted side lifting. 15.2 (pp. 336-338): dedicated and universal rigs carry a telescoping leader raised hydraulically and winch lines to offload and loft piles. 15.3 (pp. 338-347): leads keep the blow concentric; the box lead is the most common type and the swinging lead the most widely used configuration (simple, light, low cost, largest operating radius); a stabbing guide and a pile gate at the bottom keep the pile aligned. Penalizing swinging leads is not justified; they suit excavations and water. Batter alignment is harder with swinging leads, more so with diesel hammers. Fixed leads (spotter or brace) attempt true alignment but take longer to reposition; semi-fixed (vertical travel) leads move vertically at their connections; side batter needs a moonbeam; offshore leads are a short section with a pile guide and need a template. 15.4 (pp. 348-349): templates over water or excavations, top within 5 ft of cutoff or water elevation, whichever is lower, preferably at or below cutoff; a 1H:4V batter pile set at plan location on a template 5 ft above cutoff is 15 in. out at cutoff (Figure 15-17); rollers preferred. 15.5 (pp. 349-351): one-piece helmets or a base helmet with inserts; fit loosely, about 0.1 to 0.2 in. larger than the pile; alignment is critical for precast concrete. 15.6 (pp. 352-353): proprietary cushions (micarta, nylon, urethane, aluminum laminates) last up to 200 hours; hardwood, small wood pieces, wire rope, highly elastic material and asbestos are not permitted (prohibited by AASHTO); many hammers need a specific cushion thickness for timing. 15.7 (pp. 353-354): wood pile cushions at least 4 in.; after replacing a cushion the first 100 blows are not used for acceptance; a wood cushion takes 1000 to 2000 blows; use a new, dry cushion for each pile.
key_points: Crawler cranes: most common; 360 degree radius; need firm ground or crane mats
Truck and rough terrain cranes: outriggers, restricted side lifting, power source not crane mounted
Box lead is the most common lead type; swinging lead the most widely used configuration
Prohibiting swinging leads is not justified; an embedded lead bottom with a gate holds bottom alignment
Template top within 5 ft of cutoff or water elevation (lower); 1H:4V pile 15 in. out for a template 5 ft high
Helmets or inserts about 0.1 to 0.2 in. larger than the pile diameter
Proprietary hammer cushions last up to 200 hours; no hardwood, wire rope, highly elastic material or asbestos
Wood pile cushions at least 4 in. thick; new, dry cushion for each pile
After a cushion change, the first 100 blows are not used for pile acceptance
A wood pile cushion takes 1000 to 2000 blows in total

sections.title: Hammers, Drop Hammers, Air/Steam Hammers, Diesel Hammers, and Hydraulic Hammers
sections.summary: Hammers are impact, vibratory or resonant (Table 15-1). Ratings are potential energy, but losses make kinetic energy smaller and transferred energy (ENTHRU) smaller again (Eqs 15-1, 15-2). Drop hammers are not recommended for foundation piles. Air/steam hammers lose energy to preadmission; double acting and differential types are now infrequent. Open end diesel stroke follows resistance (Eq 15-3); closed end diesels use a bounce chamber gauge. Hydraulic hammers need a built-in energy monitor.
sections.body: 15.8 (pp. 355-357): impact hammers are the primary type; Table 15-1 compares types. 15.8.1 (pp. 358-359): ratings come from energy concepts; gravity hammers are rated w x h, double acting hammers by equivalent stroke; Eq 15-1 gives impact velocity and Eq 15-2 kinetic energy; friction, residual pressure, preadmission, gas compression and pre-ignition make kinetic energy less than potential; cushions and the pile head absorb more; transferred energy (ENTHRU) is the integral of force times velocity. 15.9 (pp. 359-360): drop hammers have low fall efficiency and high damage risk; limit the stroke; now mostly for sheet piles; not recommended for foundation piles. 15.10 (pp. 361-363): single acting air/steam strokes vary with pressure, volume and rebound; pressure re-enters about 2 in. before impact and a thin cushion causes preadmission; maximum stroke generally 3 to 5 ft. 15.11 (pp. 363-365): double acting hammers give comparable energy at up to about twice the blow rate, are slightly less efficient, may need reduced pressure against lift-off and are infrequent. 15.12 (pp. 366-367): differential hammers need 120 to 140 psi at the inlet (compressors give about 120 to 130 psi). 15.13 (pp. 368-370): no consensus on diesel ratings; stroke depends on fuel, rings, dampener, resistance and pile; pre-ignition; low resistance may stop the hammer; reduced fuel limits stresses; Eq 15-3 gives stroke from blow rate for single acting diesels only. 15.14 (pp. 371-373): the closed top bounce chamber shortens the stroke; fuel is reduced to avoid lift-off; energy from the bounce chamber gauge with the manufacturer's chart for the hose length. 15.15 (pp. 373-375): single acting hydraulic stroke, blow rate and dwell are adjustable; the built-in ram velocity monitor should be required. 15.16 (pp. 375-376): double acting hydraulic hammers are enclosed, so monitoring is essential; they work underwater and most have no conventional hammer cushion.
key_points: Hammer types: impact, vibratory and resonant; impact hammers are primary (Table 15-1)
Eq 15-1: Vi = sqrt(2gh); Eq 15-2: KE = (1/2) m Vi^2
Losses make kinetic energy less than potential; transferred energy ENTHRU = integral of force x velocity
Drop hammers: low efficiency, high damage risk; not recommended for foundation piles
Single acting air/steam: maximum stroke generally 3 to 5 ft; thin cushion causes preadmission
Double acting air/steam: similar energy at up to about twice the blow rate; now infrequent
Differential air/steam: needs 120 to 140 psi at the hammer inlet
Open end diesel: stroke depends on resistance; Eq 15-3 h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3 for single acting diesels only
Closed end diesel: energy from bounce chamber pressure with the manufacturer's chart for the hose length
Hydraulic hammers: built-in ram velocity monitor should be required; essential on enclosed double acting models

sections.title: Vibratory Hammers and Resonant Hammers
sections.summary: Vibratory hammers use paired counter-rotating eccentric weights. Variable moment and high frequency models run up to 2300 to 2400 vibrations per minute (40 Hz), standard up to 1600 (26 Hz), low frequency about 1200 (20 Hz); start up and shut down cause most vibration concern. Best in granular soils; not for precast concrete. No reliable method estimates resistance during vibratory or resonant installation. Resonant hammers oscillate at up to 180 Hz.
sections.body: 15.17 (pp. 375-378): paired counter-rotating eccentric weights give a sinusoidal axial force while the horizontal components cancel. Variable moment and high frequency hammers operate up to 2300 to 2400 vibrations per minute (40 Hz), standard hammers up to 1600 (26 Hz) and low frequency hammers up to about 1200 (20 Hz). The lower the rate, the greater the effect on soil and structures, so start up and shut down raise the most vibration concern; variable moment hammers reach speed with the eccentrics in neutral. Hydraulic clamps connect to the pile for installation or extraction; leads are usually not needed, though sheet pile cells often need templates. Rated by energy per second or driving force. Used for sheet piles, non-displacement H-piles and open end pipe piles; closed end and displacement piles are difficult; not for precast concrete (tensile and bending stresses). Most effective in granular soils, especially submerged; may work in silty or softer clays; less effective in stiff to hard clays. Some wave equation programs simulate vibratory driving, but no reliable technique estimates nominal resistance during installation, so it must be confirmed by other means. 15.18 (pp. 378-379): resonant hammers switch hydraulic oil across a piston at up to 180 Hz (10,800 vibrations per minute) with an algorithm that holds resonance; advantages are fast installation, very low ground vibration and reduced noise; resistance must be verified with an impact hammer and standard methods afterwards.
key_points: Vibratory: paired counter-rotating eccentric weights; horizontal components cancel
Variable moment and high frequency up to 2300-2400 vpm (40 Hz); standard up to 1600 (26 Hz); low frequency about 1200 (20 Hz)
Start up and shut down raise the most vibration concern; variable moment hammers start with eccentrics neutral
Rated by energy per second or driving force, not energy per blow
Best in granular soils, especially submerged; less effective in stiff to hard clays
Not for precast concrete piles; closed end and displacement piles are difficult
No reliable technique estimates nominal resistance during vibratory installation; confirm by other means
Resonant hammers: up to 180 Hz (10,800 vpm); fast, low vibration, less noise; verify with an impact hammer

sections.title: Impact Hammer Size Selection, Hammer Kinetic Energy Monitoring, Noise Suppression Equipment, and Underwater Noise Suppression Equipment
sections.summary: Dynamic formulas should not select hammers; the wave equation is recommended. A ram weight of 1 to 2% of the required nominal resistance or nominal driving resistance, whichever is greater, is a good first estimate; Table 15-2 gives preliminary minimum energies, not for specifications. Kinetic energy readouts use proximity switches. Driving noise is 80 to 130 dBa; shrouds cut about 10 dBa. Bubble curtains reduce underwater overpressure; over 4.4 psi has been found detrimental.
sections.body: 15.19 (pp. 379-380): too small a hammer may not reach the resistance or need excessive blows; too large may damage the pile. Dynamic formulas should not be used to select hammer energy; results worsen as hammer complexity and resistance increase. The wave equation is recommended; a ram weight of 1 to 2% of the required nominal resistance or nominal driving resistance, whichever is greater, is a good first estimate; Table 15-2 gives approximate minimum energies, to be modified for pile type, loads, lengths and soils (a smaller hammer may suit short piles to rock); not for specifications (see Chapter 14). 15.20 (pp. 380-383): factory readouts time the ram between proximity switches for impact velocity, kinetic energy, blow rate and open end diesel stroke; any hammer can be retrofitted (diesels: two 1.2 in. bore holes above the combustion chamber) with a transmitter to a wireless E-Saximeter that can also keep the driving log; useful on large projects and high resistance piles. 15.21 (p. 384): noise 80 to 130 dBa; optional devices cut about 10 dBa; combined measures (cushion material, exhaust shroud, damping compound, impact area shroud) gave 20 to 25 dBa. 15.22 (pp. 385-386): overpressures over 4.4 psi found detrimental, varying with species, size and maturity; bubble rings around one pile, bubble walls with a damping curtain around a substructure; the curtain must fully surround the driving; containment helps in tides, currents or with batter piles; a bubble ring cut overpressure from over 22 psi to under 3 psi (Longmuir and Lively 2001); a mandrel-driven pipe with an air gap gave 21 to 23 dBa reduction against 3 to 6 dBa for a typical bubble curtain on 30 in. piles (Reinhall et al. 2014).
key_points: Dynamic formulas should not be used to select hammer size; wave equation analysis is recommended
First estimate: ram weight 1 to 2% of required nominal resistance or Rndr, whichever is greater
Table 15-2 preliminary minimum rated energies: 12,000 to 42,000 ft-lbs for up to 600 kips; not for specifications
A smaller hammer may suit short piles to rock to control driving stresses
Kinetic energy readouts time the ram between proximity switches; any hammer can be retrofitted
Impact driving noise 80 to 130 dBa; manufacturer devices cut about 10 dBa; combined measures 20 to 25 dBa
Underwater overpressure over 4.4 psi found detrimental; bubble curtain must fully surround the pile
Bubble ring case: over 22 psi reduced to under 3 psi
Mandrel air gap: 21 to 23 dBa reduction against 3 to 6 dBa for a typical bubble curtain

sections.title: Followers, Jetting, Predrilling, Spudding, and Equipment Submittals
sections.summary: Followers lose energy and make alignment hard; match the pile's stiffness per unit length and avoid them when possible. Jetting is not for friction piles or piles carrying substantial lateral load; end bearing piles reach final resistance by driving. Predrilled holes are typically 4 in. less than the diagonal of square or H-piles and 1 in. less than round pile diameters. Spudding keeps cuttings off the surface. Equipment submittals let the Engineer run wave equation analyses for driving criteria.
sections.body: 15.23 (pp. 386-387): a follower transmits blows when the pile head is below the leads (under bridges, underwater, below grade); alignment, particularly of batter piles, is a problem; energy is lost in follower compression and connections, changing the blow count; losses estimated by thorough wave equation analysis or dynamic measurements; stiffness per unit length about equal to the pile's; much softer followers avoided; considerable maintenance; avoid when possible; an underwater hammer is an alternative. 15.24 (pp. 388-389): jetting with water or air, inside or outside the pile, most effective in loose to medium dense granular soils; not recommended for friction piles; avoided where substantial lateral resistance is needed; end bearing piles reach final resistance by driving without jetting; backfill open holes; separate pay item; rarely used now unless jetted material can be contained. 15.25 (pp. 389-390): predrilling through obstructions and embankments and to reduce heave of closely spaced displacement piles; hole size and depth in the contract documents; typically 4 in. less than the diagonal of square or H-piles and 1 in. less than round pile diameters; equal to the diagonal or diameter through very hard material; up to 6 in. larger than the greatest dimension in embankments; separate pay item. 15.26 (p. 390): spudding drives or drops a short strong member and removes it, useful in miscellaneous fill and debris; the spud may stick if driven too deep; cuttings and groundwater stay below ground. 15.27 (pp. 390-392): the contractor submits equipment and procedures and a Pile Installation Plan before driving; the Engineer runs wave equation analyses for preliminary or final criteria; Figure 15-50 is the drive system submittal form; without system details wave equation accuracy drops.
key_points: Followers: energy loss and alignment problems; stiffness per unit length about equal to the pile's; avoid when possible
Follower losses estimated by thorough wave equation analysis or dynamic measurements
Jetting: not for friction piles or substantial lateral resistance; end bearing piles finish by driving
Jetting is rarely used now unless jetted material can be contained
Predrill holes: 4 in. less than diagonal (square, H-piles); 1 in. less than diameter (round piles)
Predrill holes in embankments up to 6 in. larger than the greatest pile dimension
Separate pay items for jetting and predrilling when anticipated
Spudding keeps cuttings and groundwater below ground; the spud may stick if driven too deep
Equipment submittal and Pile Installation Plan let the Engineer set wave equation driving criteria
